learn.hook: Just as a sentence is made of words and punctuation, a Python statement is made of tokens. Some of those words are reserved, and you can't touch them.
points: Character set: the characters Python recognises: letters (A–Z, a–z), digits (0–9), special symbols (+ − * / ( ) [ ] { } : , ' " # etc.) and whitespace (space, tab, newline). Python 3 also accepts Unicode characters.
A token is the smallest meaningful unit of a program. Types: keywords, identifiers, literals, operators and punctuators (delimiters).
Literals are fixed values written directly in code: 25, 3.14, 'Delhi', True, None. Operators perform operations: +, ==, and. Punctuators structure the code: ( ) [ ] { } , : etc.
Keywords are reserved words with a special meaning, e.g. if, else, elif, for, while, True, False, None, and, or, not, def, import, in, is. They cannot be used as identifiers.
Keywords are case-sensitive: True is a keyword but true is not. print and input are built-in function names, not keywords.

learn.hook: Naming a variable x1 works. Naming it total_marks works better. Naming it 1st_rank crashes your code.
points: An identifier is a name given to a variable, function or other object.

Rules: it can contain letters (A–Z, a–z), digits (0–9) and underscore (_); it must start with a letter or underscore, not a digit; no spaces or special symbols like @, $, %, -, .; it cannot be a keyword; it is case-sensitive.
Good practice: use meaningful names (total_marks, not t), separate words with underscores. An identifier can be of any length.
A comment starts with # and runs to the end of the line. The interpreter ignores it; it explains code to humans.
A docstring is a string in triple quotes ("""...""") placed as the first statement of a module or function to document it.

learn.hook: In Python, a variable is not a box that holds a value. It's a name tag tied to an object in memory, and you can move the tag.
points: A variable is a name that refers to a value (object) stored in memory. Python needs no explicit declaration; a variable is created when it is first assigned.
Assignment uses =: the right side (r-value, an expression) is evaluated first, then the name on the left (l-value) is made to refer to it. 5 = x is an error because 5 cannot be an l-value.
Multiple assignment: a = b = c = 0 gives all three the value 0; x, y, z = 1, 2, 3 assigns each in turn. x, y = y, x swaps two values.
Everything in Python is an object with an identity (its location in memory), a type and a value. id(x) returns the identity; type(x) returns the type.

example.q: Trace: x = 10; y = x; x = x + 5. What are x and y?
steps: y = x: y refers to the same 10

topics.title: Data types: numbers, sequences, sets, None and dictionaries

learn.hook: Is 9876543210 a number or a string? For a phone number, you'll want a string. Picking the right type is half of programming.
points: Numbers: int (whole numbers like −5, 2026), float (with a decimal point, like 3.14, 2.0) and complex (like 3 + 4j). bool (True/False) is a subtype of int, so True + True = 2.
Sequences (ordered collections): str (characters in quotes, 'India'), list (in square brackets, mutable, [1, 'a', 2.5]) and tuple (in parentheses, immutable, (10, 20)).
Set: an unordered collection of unique items in braces, e.g. {1, 2, 3}; duplicates are removed automatically.
None: a special value meaning absence of a value; its type is NoneType.
Mapping: a dictionary (dict) stores key : value pairs in braces, e.g. {'roll': 12, 'name': 'Asha'}.

example.answer: int, float, str, list, tuple, set, dict, bool, NoneType, complex

learn.reallife: A UPI transaction record might use a str for the UPI ID, a float for the amount, a bool for success and a dict to bundle them together.

topics.title: Mutable vs immutable, and choosing a data type

learn.hook: You can change a list in place but not a string. Try s[0] = 'J' on 'Python' and Python refuses. Why?
points: Mutable types can be changed in place after creation: list, dictionary, set. Their id() stays the same when you modify their contents.
Immutable types cannot be changed in place: int, float, bool, complex, str, tuple. 'Changing' them actually creates a new object; the variable then refers to the new object (a different id).
Example: x = 10; x = x + 1 makes x refer to a NEW object 11. L = [1, 2]; L.append(3) changes the SAME list.

Choosing types: use a list for a collection that will change (shopping cart), a tuple for fixed data (days of the week, coordinates), a dictionary for fast lookup by key (roll number → name), a set for unique items, and type() to check a value's type.

example.q: Predict: L = [1, 2]; before = id(L); L.append(3); is id(L) == before? And for s = 'ab'; before = id(s); s = s + 'c'?

s + 'c' creates a new string 'abc'; s now refers to it → ids differ → False
example.answer: List: True (same object). String: False (new object).

learn.hook: 7 / 2 is 3.5, 7 // 2 is 3, and −7 // 2 is −4, not −3. Python's operators have a few surprises worth knowing.
points: Arithmetic: + − * (multiply), / (true division, always a float), // (floor division: rounds DOWN to the nearest whole number), % (remainder/modulus), ** (exponent).
With ints, +, −, *, //, % give an int; / always gives a float (10 / 2 is 5.0). If either operand is a float, the result is a float (7.0 // 2 is 3.0).
Floor division rounds towards minus infinity: −7 // 2 is −4. The remainder takes the sign of the divisor: −7 % 2 is 1, 7 % −2 is −1.
Relational operators ==, !=, >, <, >=, <= compare values and return True or False. Note: = assigns, == compares.
Augmented assignment: x += 3 means x = x + 3. Similarly −=, *=, /=, %=, //=, **=.

What is the output?

quiz.explain: Floor division rounds down towards minus infinity: −3.5 becomes −4.

quiz.mistake: Uses / instead of // for //=

options: = assigns a value; == compares two values and gives True or False
quiz.explain: x = 5 stores 5 in x; x == 5 asks whether x equals 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses = for comparison as in maths

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 7 / 2 and 7 // 2 are the same. Explain Python's arithmetic, relational and assignment operators.

learn.hook: 0 or 'Guest' gives 'Guest'. In Python, and/or don't always return True or False; they return one of the operands!
points: Logical operators: and (True only if both are True), or (True if at least one is True), not (reverses). They short-circuit: evaluation stops as soon as the result is known.
Truth values: 0, 0.0, '' (empty string), [], (), {}, None and False are falsy; everything else is truthy.
With non-Boolean operands: x and y returns x if x is falsy, else y. x or y returns x if x is truthy, else y. not always returns True or False. e.g. 0 or 5 → 5; 3 and 0 → 0; 5 and 7 → 7.
Identity operators: is and is not check whether two names refer to the SAME object (same id), not just equal values.
Membership operators: in and not in test whether a value is present in a sequence (string, list, tuple) or is a key of a dictionary.

example.q: Evaluate: (a) 'a' in 'Delhi' (b) 3 not in [1, 2, 3] (c) 0 or 'Guest' (d) not 0
steps: (b) 3 is in the list, so 'not in' gives False
(c) 0 is falsy, so or returns the second operand → 'Guest'

learn.reallife: A login check might be: if user in registered_users and password == saved_password: — membership and logic together.

What is the output?
print(5 and 7)
quiz.explain: 5 is truthy, so 'and' returns its second operand, 7.

learn.hook: 2 ** 3 ** 2 is 512, not 64. Knowing which operator goes first is the difference between full marks and zero.
points: An expression is a combination of values, variables and operators that Python evaluates to a single value: 3 + 4 * 2, x > 5, 'a' * 3.
Precedence (highest first): ( ) parentheses → ** → unary −, + → * / // % → binary + − → relational (==, !=, <, >, <=, >=) → not → and → or.
Associativity: operators of equal precedence are evaluated left to right, EXCEPT ** which is right to left: 2 ** 3 ** 2 = 2 ** 9 = 512.
Since ** binds tighter than unary minus, −2 ** 2 = −(2 ** 2) = −4. Use parentheses (−2) ** 2 = 4 when you mean it.
A statement is a unit of code that Python executes, e.g. x = 5, print(x), if ...: An expression produces a value; a statement performs an action (an expression can be part of a statement).

points: Explicit conversion (type casting) is done by the programmer using functions: int(), float(), str(), chr(), ord(), and also list(), tuple(), bool().

Implicit conversion (coercion) is done automatically by Python to avoid data loss: int + float gives float (5 + 2.0 = 7.0); True + 1 = 2.
Python does NOT implicitly convert between str and numbers: '5' + 2 raises TypeError.

topics.title: Debugging: syntax, logical and runtime errors

learn.hook: The program runs, no red text, but your average of 80 and 90 comes out as 125. That's the sneakiest kind of bug.
points: Debugging is the process of finding and removing errors (bugs) from a program.
Syntax error: the code breaks the rules of the language (missing colon, unmatched bracket, misspelt keyword). Python refuses to run the program. e.g. print('Hi' → SyntaxError.

Logical error: the program runs without crashing but gives the wrong output because the logic is wrong, e.g. average = a + b / 2 instead of (a + b) / 2. Python gives no message, so these are hardest to find.

Runtime error (exception): the program starts but stops during execution, e.g. ZeroDivisionError (10 / 0), ValueError (int('abc')), TypeError ('5' + 2), NameError (using an undefined name), IndexError.
Exam tasks: identify valid identifiers, evaluate expressions, predict output, name the error type, and write small programs.

example.q: Classify: (a) if x > 5 print(x)  (b) avg = a + b / 2  (c) print(10 / n) with n = 0

(c) Starts running, then crashes when dividing by zero → runtime error (ZeroDivisionError)

topics.title: Flow of control, if and if-else

learn.hook: An ATM doesn't give cash to everyone. It checks: is the PIN right? Is there enough balance? Every check is an if.
points: Flow of control is the order in which statements of a program are executed.
Three structures: sequential (statements one after another), selection/conditional (choose a path using a condition) and iteration/repetition (repeat statements in a loop).
if statement: if condition: followed by an indented block. The block runs only when the condition is True; otherwise it is skipped.
if-else: if condition: block1 else: block2. Exactly one of the two blocks runs. The colon (:) after if and else is compulsory.
Flowchart: a decision diamond with a True path leading to the if-block and a False path leading to the else-block (or past the if-block).

items: In if-else, both blocks can run for one input.

If the condition is False, the block is simply skipped.
Selection chooses between paths; repetition repeats.
The else block runs when the if condition is False.

topics.title: elif ladders, nested if and indentation

learn.hook: Grades A, B, C, D, E… Instead of five separate ifs, Python gives you a ladder: if, elif, elif, else.
points: if-elif-else ladder: conditions are checked from top to bottom; the FIRST True condition's block runs and the rest are skipped. else (optional) runs if none is True.
Because checking stops at the first True condition, the order of conditions matters: check marks >= 90 before marks >= 75.
Nested if: an if (or if-else) placed inside another if's block, for decisions that depend on earlier decisions.
Indentation (leading spaces, usually 4) marks which statements belong to a block. All statements in a block must have the same indentation.
Inconsistent or missing indentation gives IndentationError (a kind of syntax error).

example.q: Find the grade for marks = 82 using: >= 90 'A', >= 75 'B', >= 60 'C', else 'D'.

learn.reallife: Income tax slabs are a classic elif ladder: if income falls in slab 1, tax rate X; elif slab 2, rate Y; and so on.

games.title: Ladder logic
items: In an elif ladder, more than one block can run.
Only the first True condition's block runs.
The else at the end of an elif ladder is optional.
Without it, nothing runs if all conditions are False.
Python uses indentation to group statements into blocks.
There are no braces; indentation defines blocks.
Mixing indentation levels inside one block causes IndentationError.
All statements in a block need the same indentation.
An if cannot be placed inside another if.
That is a nested if, which is allowed.

learn.hook: Printing a table of 7 with ten print statements is boring. A for loop does it in two lines, for any number.
points: Loops repeat a set of statements, so we don't write the same code again and again.
for variable in sequence: runs the block once for each item of the sequence (a string, list, tuple or range), in order.
range(stop) gives 0 to stop − 1. range(start, stop) gives start to stop − 1. range(start, stop, step) moves by step. The stop value is never included.
Negative step counts down: range(10, 0, −2) gives 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. If the range is empty (e.g. range(5, 1)), the loop body doesn't run.
Programs: print 1 to n; even numbers with range(2, n + 1, 2); multiplication table: for i in range(1, 11): print(n, 'x', i, '=', n * i); sum of first n numbers with total += i.

learn.hook: You don't know how many digits a number has, so you can't use a fixed range. A while loop keeps going until the job is done.
points: while condition: repeats its block as long as the condition is True. The condition is checked before every iteration; if it is False at the start, the block never runs.
A while loop needs: (1) a loop variable initialised before the loop, (2) a condition using it, (3) an update inside the loop that moves it towards making the condition False.
If the update is missing or wrong, the condition never becomes False: an infinite loop. e.g. i = 1; while i <= 5: print(i) (no i += 1).
Digit programs use n % 10 to get the last digit and n // 10 to remove it: sum of digits, reverse a number (rev = rev * 10 + digit).
Factorial: f = 1; while n > 1: f *= n; n −= 1. HCF by Euclid: while b != 0: a, b = b, a % b, then a is the HCF.

example.q: Reverse the number 472 using a while loop.

learn.reallife: An OTP screen keeps asking 'while attempts < 3 and OTP is wrong'. It doesn't know in advance how many tries you'll need.

The remainder on dividing by 10 is the units digit.
A while loop always runs at least once.

topics.title: break, continue, pass and loop else

learn.hook: Searching for your roll number in a list of 500? Once you find it, stop. That's break.
points: break immediately exits the innermost loop; control goes to the first statement after the loop.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration of the loop.
A loop can have an else clause. It runs when the loop finishes normally (condition becomes False or the sequence ends), but NOT if the loop was ended by break.
pass does nothing. It is a placeholder where a statement is required by syntax but no action is needed yet, e.g. an empty if-block.
Prime check with break: for i in range(2, n): if n % i == 0: print('Not prime'); break — else: print('Prime'). The loop's else runs only if no divisor was found.

steps: Because of break, the loop's else does not run

learn.reallife: A UPI app scanning recent transactions for a suspicious one uses break as soon as it finds it, and continue to skip transactions already verified.

items: continue only skips the rest of the current iteration.

learn.hook: A clock's minute hand goes round 60 times for every turn of the hour hand. That's a nested loop.
points: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For every single iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely.
Total inner iterations = outer count × inner count (when the inner range is fixed). e.g. for i in range(3): for j in range(4) → 12 runs.
Patterns: the outer loop controls rows; the inner loop controls what is printed in each row. Use print(..., end='') inside and print() after the inner loop to move to the next line.
Primes in a range: an outer loop over numbers and an inner loop over possible divisors (with break and loop else).
Series like 1 + x + x² + … + xⁿ: loop i from 0 to n, add x ** i. Exam tasks: predict output, convert a for loop to while, count iterations.

example.q:
Print this triangle:
*
**
***
steps: for j in range(i):  # i stars in row i

learn.reallife: A cinema booking screen draws its seat grid with nested loops: rows A to M outside, seat numbers 1 to 20 inside.

quiz.mistake: Prints i (the row number) instead of j

learn.hook: 'Chandrayaan' has 11 characters, and Python can reach any of them instantly, from the front or from the back.
points: A string is a sequence of Unicode characters enclosed in single ('…'), double ("…") or triple quotes ('''…''' or """…"""). Triple quotes allow multi-line strings.
Each character has an index. Positive indexing starts at 0 from the left; negative indexing starts at −1 from the right. For s = 'INDIA': s[0] = 'I', s[4] = 'A', s[−1] = 'A', s[−5] = 'I'.
For a string of length n, valid indices are 0 to n − 1 and −1 to −n. Any other index raises IndexError. The index must be an integer: s[1.5] raises TypeError.
Strings are immutable: you cannot change a character in place. s[0] = 'J' raises TypeError. To 'change' a string, build a new one, e.g. s = 'J' + s[1:].

example.q: For city = 'Kolkata', find city[2], city[−1], city[−3] and the valid index range.
steps: Indices: K0 o1 l2 k3 a4 t5 a6

learn.reallife: Your PAN has a fixed pattern: the 4th character (index 3) tells the holder type, e.g. 'P' for an individual. Code reads it with pan[3].

learn.hook: 'Jai' + ' ' + 'Hind' joins strings; 'Ha' * 3 laughs three times. Strings have their own arithmetic.
points: Concatenation (+) joins two strings end to end: 'Good' + 'Day' → 'GoodDay'. Both operands must be strings; 'Age' + 15 raises TypeError.
Repetition (*) repeats a string a whole number of times: 'ab' * 3 → 'ababab'. 'ab' * 0 → '' (empty). 'ab' * 2.5 raises TypeError.
Membership: in returns True if the substring is present; not in returns True if it is absent. It is case-sensitive: 'a' in 'INDIA' is False.
Neither + nor * changes the original string; they create new strings.

learn.hook: s[::-1] reverses any string in one move. Slicing is the most-asked string skill in CBSE output questions.
points: s[m:n] gives the characters from index m up to but NOT including index n.
If m is omitted it starts at 0; if n is omitted it goes to the end. s[:] is the whole string. Slicing never raises IndexError; out-of-range limits are simply clipped.
s[m:n:k] takes every k-th character from m (k is the step). s[::2] gives characters at even indices.
Negative indices work too: s[−3:] gives the last 3 characters. A negative step moves right to left: s[::−1] reverses the string.
With a negative step, the start should be to the right of the stop: 'PYTHON'[4:1:−1] = 'OHT'. If the direction is wrong, the result is the empty string ''.

steps: Indices: C0 O1 M2 P3 U4 T5 E6 R7

learn.reallife: A PIN code like '302017' can be sliced: pin[:1] is the postal region digit and pin[:3] the sorting district, which is how mail is routed across India.

learn.hook: To count the vowels in a sentence, you have to visit every character one by one. That visit is called traversal.
points: len(s) returns the number of characters in s, including spaces and punctuation. len('') is 0.
Traversal with for: for ch in s: … gives each character in order. Simple and clean when you don't need the index.
Traversal with an index: for i in range(len(s)): … s[i] …, useful when you need positions.
Traversal with while: i = 0; while i < len(s): … s[i] …; i += 1. Forgetting i += 1 makes an infinite loop; using i <= len(s) causes IndexError.

topics.title: String methods: case, count, find, index, startswith, endswith

learn.hook: 'virat kohli'.title() gives 'Virat Kohli'. String methods do in one word what would take a loop to code.
points: Case methods return NEW strings: upper(), lower(), title() (first letter of every word capital), capitalize() (only the first character of the string capital, the rest lower), swapcase() (swaps upper and lower case).
count(sub) returns how many times sub occurs (non-overlapping). count(sub, start, end) counts within a range.
find(sub) returns the lowest index where sub starts, or −1 if not found; find(sub, start) begins searching at start. index(sub) works the same but raises ValueError if not found.
startswith(prefix) and endswith(suffix) return True/False, e.g. checking if an email ends with '@gmail.com'.

example.q: For s = 'banana', find s.count('a'), s.find('n'), s.find('x'), s.upper().

learn.reallife: Indian vehicle numbers like 'MH12AB1234' can be checked with startswith('MH') to find vehicles registered in Maharashtra.

topics.title: Testing, stripping, replace, join, partition and split

learn.hook: Users type '  9876543210 ' with stray spaces. strip() cleans it and isdigit() checks it: two methods, one valid mobile number.
points: Testing methods return True/False: isalnum() (letters or digits only), isalpha() (letters only), isdigit() (digits only), islower(), isupper(), isspace() (only whitespace), istitle(). For an empty string, isalnum(), isalpha(), isdigit() and isspace() are all False.
lstrip() removes leading whitespace, rstrip() removes trailing whitespace, strip() removes both. With an argument, e.g. strip('*'), they remove those characters instead.
replace(old, new) replaces every occurrence of old with new and returns a new string.
split(sep) breaks a string into a LIST of parts (default: split on whitespace). sep.join(list_of_strings) does the reverse: '-'.join(['a', 'b']) → 'a-b'.
partition(sep) splits at the FIRST occurrence of sep into a tuple of 3: (before, sep, after). If sep is absent: (s, '', '').

example.q: For d = '15-08-1947', find d.split('-'), '/'.join(d.split('-')), d.partition('-').

learn.reallife: Online forms on government portals use strip() to clean inputs and isdigit() to check PIN codes before accepting them.

quiz.q:
What is the output?
print('Red,Green,Blue'.split(','))
quiz.explain: split(',') returns a list of the parts between commas.
quiz.mistake: Thinks split returns a tuple or a single string

quiz.q:
What is the output?
print('user@mail.com'.partition('@'))
quiz.explain: partition returns a 3-tuple: before, separator, after.
quiz.mistake: Confuses partition with split

quiz.q:
What is the output?
print('-'.join(['2026', '11', '05']))
quiz.explain: join puts '-' between the strings in the list.
quiz.mistake: Thinks join adds no separator

quiz.explain: replace changes every 'a' to '*'.
quiz.mistake: Thinks replace changes only the first occurrence

quiz.explain: 'Class 11' has a space, so isalnum() is False; 'Class11' is all letters and digits.
quiz.mistake: Thinks spaces are allowed in isalnum()

quiz.mistake: Expects an error or a list

teach.ask: Gappu has a messy string '  15-08-1947  '. Explain strip(), split(), join(), partition(), replace() and the is-methods.
teach.praise: strip cleans the edges, split makes a list, join glues it back, partition cuts at the first separator and is-methods test the content. Toolbox complete!

topics.title: String programs: counting, replacing vowels, reversing

learn.hook: Can you reverse 'Mississippi' without [::-1]? Board examiners love asking exactly that.
points: Count a character without count(): c = 0; for ch in s: if ch == target: c += 1.
Replace all vowels with a symbol: build a new string, r = ''; for ch in s: if ch in 'aeiouAEIOU': r += '*' else: r += ch.
Reverse without slicing: (1) r = ''; for ch in s: r = ch + r, or (2) for i in range(len(s) − 1, −1, −1): r += s[i].
Since strings are immutable, these programs always build a NEW string with += rather than editing s.

example.q: Reverse 'Agra' using the index loop.

learn.reallife: Apps that mask parts of a username or phone number for privacy, like 98******10, build the masked text character by character in exactly this way.

for ch in s:

quiz.mistake: Miscounts the repeated letters

quiz.explain: Every vowel (u, a, a) is replaced by '*'; other characters are copied.
quiz.mistake: Replaces consonants instead

for ch in s:

print(r)
quiz.explain: Each character is added to the front, which reverses the string.

quiz.explain: The index goes 2, 1, 0, collecting n, o, P.
quiz.mistake: Starts the range at len(s)

quiz.mistake: Thinks join adds the separator at the end too

s is deleted after the loop
Strings are immutable, so their characters cannot be changed in place

quiz.mistake: Thinks it's just a style choice

teach.ask: Gappu must reverse a string without using slicing. Explain how to do it, and how to count a character without count().

teach.nudge: Good. How do we build the reversed string character by character?

topics.title: Palindromes, character counts and menu-driven string programs

learn.hook: MALAYALAM reads the same both ways, and so does the number 12321. Checking a palindrome is a favourite board-exam program.
points: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards: 'madam', 'level', 'MALAYALAM'. Check with s == s[::-1], or compare s[i] with s[len(s) − 1 − i] for i up to half the length.
Case matters: 'Madam' is not equal to its reverse 'madaM' unless you convert with lower() first.
Counting categories: for ch in s, use ch.isupper(), ch.islower(), ch.isdigit(), ch in 'aeiouAEIOU' (vowel), and ch.isalpha() but not a vowel (consonant). Words: len(s.split()).
A menu-driven program shows options (1. Length 2. Reverse 3. Exit), reads a choice, and uses an if-elif ladder inside a while loop until Exit is chosen.
Exam tasks: predict outputs of slicing and methods; write programs that count, reverse, check palindromes or replace characters.

example.q: Check whether 'Level' is a palindrome, ignoring case.

learn.reallife: Text-processing tools used in Indian-language apps count vowels, consonants and words in exactly this way to build spell-checkers and word-count features.

quiz.explain: 'level' reversed is 'level', so they are equal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the comparison needs a loop

quiz.explain: 'Madam' reversed is 'madaM'; 'M' and 'm' differ, so they're not equal.
quiz.mistake: Ignores case

What is the output?

quiz.explain: Uppercase: I, P (2). Lowercase: n, d, i, a (4). Digits: 2, 6 (2).
quiz.mistake: Counts the uppercase letters as lowercase too

quiz.explain: split() gives ['Unity', 'in', 'diversity', 'is', 'strength'], 5 words.
quiz.mistake: Counts spaces instead of words

quiz.q: Which condition checks whether string s is a palindrome, ignoring case?
quiz.explain: Both sides must be converted to the same case before comparing.
quiz.mistake: Converts only one side, or checks only the end characters

quiz.explain: Converting the number to a string lets us compare it with its reverse.

teach.ask: Gappu wants a program that says whether a word is a palindrome and counts its vowels. Explain how.
teach.praise: Compare the lowercase word with its reverse for palindromes, and loop with checks to count vowels. Two programs in one!

learn.hook: A cricket team sheet changes after every match: one player out, one in. A Python list is built for exactly that kind of changing data.
points: A list is an ordered sequence of elements in square brackets, separated by commas: marks = [78, 92, 65]. Elements can be of mixed types: ['Asha', 16, 5.4, True]. [] is an empty list.
Indexing works like strings: positive from 0 (left), negative from −1 (right). L[len(L)] raises IndexError.
Lists are mutable: you can change an element in place with L[i] = new_value; the list object stays the same.
A list can contain other lists (nested lists), e.g. [[1, 2], [3, 4]].

example.q: team = ['Rohit', 'Virat', 'Rahul', 'Hardik']. Replace 'Rahul' with 'Pant' and find team[−1].

learn.reallife: A school's attendance app keeps today's absentees in a list and updates it as late-comers arrive.

games.title: List basics
items: Elements can be changed in place.
All elements of a list must be of the same type.
L[-1] is the last element of L.
Negative indexing starts at −1 from the right.
It has no elements; len([]) is 0.
Valid indices are 0, 1, 2; L[3] raises IndexError.

teach.ask: Gappu keeps his friends' names in a list and wants to change one. Explain what a list is, indexing and mutability.
teach.praise: A list is an ordered, mutable collection in square brackets, so I can change friends[2] directly!
teach.nudge: Good. How do we reach an element, and can we change it after the list is made?

learn.hook: Joining two playlists, repeating a pattern, checking if a song exists, picking songs 3 to 7: four list operations cover it all.
points: Concatenation: L1 + L2 joins two lists into a new list. Both operands must be lists: [1, 2] + 3 raises TypeError; use [1, 2] + [3].
Repetition: L * n repeats the list n times: [0] * 4 → [0, 0, 0, 0].
Membership: x in L is True if x is an element of L; not in is the opposite. 2 in [[1, 2], 3] is False because 2 is inside a sub-list, not an element.
Slicing works like strings: L[m:n], L[m:n:k], L[::−1] (reversed copy). Slices return new lists; out-of-range limits are clipped.
learn.reallife: An IPL fantasy app joins your batsmen and bowlers lists with + and checks 'player in my_team' before letting you pick someone twice.

What is the output?

quiz.explain: + joins the two lists into one longer list.
quiz.mistake: Adds the elements pairwise

quiz.q:
What is the output?
print(['Hi'] * 3)
quiz.explain: * repeats the list's elements three times.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the string inside is repeated

What is the output?
print([1, 2] + 3)
quiz.explain: A list can only be concatenated with another list.
quiz.mistake: Thinks + appends a number

L = ['a', 'b', 'c', 'd', 'e', 'f']
print(L[1:5:2])
quiz.explain: Indices 1 and 3 (step 2, stop 5 excluded).

L = [1, 2, 3]
print(L[5:10])

Reason (R): Slicing creates and returns a new list.

Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A

A is false but R is true

teach.ask: Gappu wants to join two lists and pick out a part of one. Explain +, *, in and slicing on lists.
teach.praise: + joins, * repeats, in checks membership and slices pick parts as new lists. List power!
teach.nudge: Good. What do + and * do with lists, and what does a slice return?

learn.hook: To total 40 students' marks you need to visit each one. Traversal is how every list program begins.
points: Traversal by element: for x in L: … gives each element in order.
Traversal by index: for i in range(len(L)): … L[i] …, needed when you want positions or want to modify elements.
Traversal with while: i = 0; while i < len(L): …; i += 1.
len(L) gives the number of elements. list() builds a list from a sequence: list('abc') → ['a', 'b', 'c'], list((1, 2)) → [1, 2], list(range(3)) → [0, 1, 2]; list() alone gives [].

steps: Need indices to modify: for i in range(len(L)):

What is the output?

teach.ask: Gappu wants to add 5 bonus marks to every element of his list. Explain how to traverse a list, and why the index matters here.
teach.praise: To change elements I must loop over indices with range(len(L)) and assign L[i]. A plain 'for x in L' only reads them!
teach.nudge: Good. Why doesn't 'for x in L: x += 5' change the list? What should we loop over instead?

topics.title: Adding elements: append, extend, insert; count and index

learn.hook: append([4, 5]) and extend([4, 5]) look similar but give very different lists. This is a CBSE favourite.
points: append(x) adds x as ONE element at the end: [1, 2].append([3, 4]) → [1, 2, [3, 4]].
extend(iterable) adds EACH element of the iterable at the end: [1, 2].extend([3, 4]) → [1, 2, 3, 4]. extend('ab') adds 'a' and 'b'.
insert(i, x) inserts x before index i: [10, 30].insert(1, 20) → [10, 20, 30]. If i is beyond the end, x goes at the end.
count(x) returns how many times x occurs. index(x) returns the index of the first occurrence; ValueError if x is not present.
append, extend and insert change the list in place and return None, so print(L.append(5)) prints None.

example.q: L = [1, 2]. Do L.append([3]), then L.extend([4, 5]), then L.insert(0, 0). What is L and len(L)?

learn.reallife: When a new student joins mid-year, the school roll list uses insert() to place the name in alphabetical position, and count() to check for duplicate entries.

games.title: Method facts
items: append() can add several separate elements at once.
append adds exactly one element (which may itself be a list).
L.index(x) raises ValueError if x is not in L.
Unlike string find(), there is no −1 result.
L.count(x) returns the number of occurrences of x.
Elements from index 1 onwards shift right.
append returns None, so None is printed.

L.append([3, 4])
print(L, len(L))
quiz.explain: append adds the list [3, 4] as a single element, so the length is 3.
quiz.mistake: Confuses append with extend

quiz.q:
What is the output?
L = [1, 2]
L.extend([3, 4])
print(L, len(L))
quiz.explain: extend adds 3 and 4 as separate elements.
quiz.mistake: Confuses extend with append

quiz.q:
What is the output?
L = ['a', 'b', 'c']
L.insert(1, 'x')
print(L)
quiz.explain: insert(1, 'x') places 'x' at index 1 and shifts the rest right.
quiz.mistake: Replaces the element instead of inserting

quiz.q:
What is the output?
L = [1, 2]
print(L.append(3))
quiz.explain: append changes the list but returns None.
quiz.mistake: Expects append to return the new list

quiz.q:
What is the output?
L = [2, 5, 7, 5, 5]
print(L.count(5), L.index(5))
quiz.explain: 5 occurs 3 times; its first occurrence is at index 1.
quiz.mistake: Gives the last occurrence or counts from 1

quiz.q:
What is the output?
L = [10, 20]
print(L.index(30))
quiz.explain: index raises ValueError when the element is absent.
quiz.mistake: Applies the string find() rule to lists

quiz.q:
What is the output?
L = [1, 2]
L.extend('hi')
print(L)
quiz.explain: extend adds each character of the string separately.
quiz.mistake: Thinks extend adds the whole string as one element

quiz.q:
What is the output?
L = [5, 10]
L.insert(50, 99)
print(L)
quiz.explain: An insert position beyond the end simply adds the element at the end.
quiz.mistake: Expects an IndexError

learn.hook: L.sort() and sorted(L) both sort, but only one of them leaves your original list alone. Mixing them up is a classic bug.
points: remove(x) deletes the FIRST occurrence of x (ValueError if absent). pop(i) removes and RETURNS the element at index i; pop() with no index removes the last. del L[i] or del L[m:n] deletes by index/slice. clear() empties the list.
reverse() reverses the list in place. sort() sorts in place in ascending order; sort(reverse=True) sorts in descending order. Both return None.
sorted(L) returns a NEW sorted list and leaves L unchanged. sorted(L, reverse=True) for descending order.
min(L), max(L) and sum(L) work on lists of numbers (min and max also on strings, comparing alphabetically by character codes).

example.q: L = [40, 10, 30, 20]. Find sorted(L), then L after L.sort(reverse=True), then L.pop() and sum(L) after that.

learn.hook: You 'copy' a list with B = A, change B, and A changes too! That's not a bug in Python; it's an alias.
points: A nested list contains lists as elements, like a table: M = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]. M[i] is row i, and M[i][j] is the element in row i, column j. M[1][2] = 6.
Assignment B = A does NOT copy: both names refer to the SAME list (an alias). Changing B[0] changes A[0] too, and B is A is True.
True (shallow) copies are separate list objects: B = A[:], B = list(A), B = A.copy(), or import copy; B = copy.copy(A).
After a true copy, B is A is False and changing B's elements does not affect A (for simple elements).
learn.reallife: A cinema seat map is a nested list: seats[row][col] = 'X' marks a booked seat. And a booking app copies the map before trying changes, so a failed payment doesn't mess up the real one.

teach.ask: Gappu wrote B = A to back up his list, changed B and lost the original. Explain aliasing, true copies and nested lists.

topics.title: Lists and functions, and menu-driven list programs

learn.hook: Pass a list to a function, change it inside, and the change is still there after the function returns. Lists travel by reference.
points: When a list is passed to a function, the parameter refers to the SAME list object as the argument.
So changes made through the parameter (L[i] = …, L.append(…), L.sort()) are visible in the original list after the function returns, because lists are mutable.
But if the parameter is REASSIGNED to a new list inside the function (L = [0, 0]), it now refers to a different object, and the original list is not affected.
Menu-driven program: a while loop shows a menu (1. Append 2. Insert 3. Delete 4. Modify 5. Sort 6. Display 7. Exit), reads a choice and uses an if-elif ladder to perform the chosen list operation.

steps: L and marks refer to the same list

topics.title: List programs: max, min, mean, linear search and frequency

learn.hook: Linear search is how you find your name on a printed result sheet: start at the top and check each line until you find it.
points: Max/min without built-ins: big = L[0]; for x in L: if x > big: big = x (similarly for small). Mean = sum(L) / len(L).
Linear search: check each element in order; if L[i] == key, report position i + 1 (1-based) and stop. If the loop ends without finding it, report 'not found'.
In the worst case (key at the end or absent), linear search makes len(L) comparisons.
Frequency of an element: L.count(x), or a loop with a counter. Frequency of every element: loop over unique elements and count each.
Exam tasks: predict outputs of list operations, and write list programs (search, max/min/mean, frequency, menu-driven operations).

steps: i = 2: 42 = 42 → found at index 2, i.e. position 3
Stop (break): only the first occurrence is reported

learn.hook: The GPS coordinates of India Gate, (28.6129, 77.2295), should never change by accident. Tuples are Python's locked boxes.
points: A tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence written in parentheses: t = (10, 'Goa', 3.5). The parentheses are optional: t = 10, 20 also makes a tuple. () is an empty tuple.
A single-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (5,) is a tuple, but (5) is just the int 5.
Indexing works as in strings and lists: t[0] is the first element, t[−1] the last; out-of-range indices raise IndexError.

Tuples are immutable: t[0] = 1 raises TypeError, and there is no append() or remove(). But if a tuple contains a mutable object such as a list, that list's contents can change: t = (1, [2, 3]); t[1].append(4) is allowed.
Prefer tuples for fixed data that must not change (days of the week, coordinates, records); they are also slightly faster to iterate over than lists.

example.q: t = ('Mon', 'Tue', 'Wed', 'Thu', 'Fri'). Find t[1], t[−2] and say what t[0] = 'Sun' does.
steps: t[0] = 'Sun' raises TypeError: tuples cannot be modified

learn.reallife: A railway timetable stores each train's fixed route as a tuple of station codes, e.g. ('NDLS', 'CNB', 'PRYJ', 'DDU'), so no program can reorder it by mistake.

t[-1] gives the last element of tuple t.

teach.ask: Gappu wonders why we need tuples if we have lists. Explain what a tuple is, the single-element rule and immutability.
teach.praise: A tuple is an immutable sequence for fixed data, and (5,) needs that comma. Lists for changing data, tuples for locked data!

learn.hook: You can't change a tuple, but you can join, repeat, slice and search it. Every one of these makes a NEW tuple.
points: Concatenation: (1, 2) + (3,) → (1, 2, 3). Both operands must be tuples; (1, 2) + 3 raises TypeError.
Repetition: ('Hi',) * 3 → ('Hi', 'Hi', 'Hi'). Membership: 3 in (1, 2, 3) → True. Slicing: t[1:3], t[::−1] return new tuples.
len(t) gives the number of elements; tuple(seq) converts a sequence: tuple('abc') → ('a', 'b', 'c'), tuple([1, 2]) → (1, 2).
t.count(x) counts occurrences; t.index(x) gives the first index of x (ValueError if absent).
sorted(t) returns a sorted LIST (not a tuple). min(t), max(t) and sum(t) work on numeric tuples.

example.q: For t = (5, 2, 8, 2, 9), find t[1:4], t.count(2), sorted(t), sum(t).

learn.reallife: Monthly temperature readings for Delhi stored as a tuple can be summarised with max(), min() and sum() without risking any change to the official data.

learn.hook: a, b = b, a swaps two values in one line, no third variable needed. That's tuple assignment.
points: Tuple assignment (unpacking): (x, y, z) = (1, 2, 3) or x, y, z = 1, 2, 3 assigns each value to the matching variable in order.
Swapping: a, b = b, a. The right side is evaluated first into a tuple (b, a), then unpacked.
The number of variables on the left must equal the number of values: a, b = (1, 2, 3) raises ValueError (too many values to unpack); a, b, c = (1, 2) raises ValueError (not enough values).
A nested tuple contains tuples as elements, e.g. student records: st = ((101, 'Asha', 92), (102, 'Ravi', 85)). st[1][1] is 'Ravi'.
Loop over records with unpacking: for roll, name, marks in st: print(roll, name, marks).

Reason (R): The right-hand side is evaluated completely into a tuple before any assignment happens.
options: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Because (b, a) is built first, assigning it doesn't lose either value.
quiz.mistake: Thinks assignments happen one at a time from left to right

teach.ask: Gappu swaps values with a third variable and wants a shortcut. Explain tuple assignment, its rule about counts, and nested tuples.
teach.praise: a, b = b, a swaps instantly, the counts must match or it's a ValueError, and nested tuples hold records. Neat!
teach.nudge: Good. What must be true about the number of variables and values in tuple assignment?

learn.hook: A function can return two answers at once, like a circle's area AND circumference, packed neatly in a tuple.
points: Swap two numbers using tuple assignment: a, b = b, a.
A function can return several values as a tuple: return area, circumference; then unpack: a, c = circle(r).
Min, max and mean of tuple values: min(t), max(t), sum(t) / len(t).
Linear search in a tuple: loop with an index and compare each element with the key; report position or 'not found'.
Frequency of elements: for each unique element, use t.count(x), or count in a loop.

example.q: Write a function that returns the area and circumference of a circle of radius 7 (use π = 22/7).

learn.reallife: An exam portal returns (total, percentage, grade) as one tuple for each student, so the report-card program can unpack all three at once.

teach.nudge: Good. How can one function return two values, and how do we receive them?

learn.hook: Your phone's contact list maps names to numbers. You never search by position; you search by name. That's a dictionary.
points: A dictionary is a mutable mapping of key : value pairs in braces: d = {'roll': 12, 'name': 'Asha'}. Keys must be unique and immutable (str, int, float, tuple); values can be anything.
Create with {} (empty), with literal pairs, or with dict(): dict(name='Asha', roll=12) or dict([('a', 1), ('b', 2)]).
Access a value by its key: d['name'] → 'Asha'. A missing key raises KeyError. Dictionaries are not indexed by position.
Add a new pair: d['class'] = 11. Modify an existing value: d['roll'] = 15. Assigning to an existing key replaces its value (keys stay unique).
A list cannot be a key (it is mutable): {[1, 2]: 'x'} raises TypeError.

example.q: Start with d = {'Asha': 92}. Add Ravi with 85, change Asha to 95, then print d.
steps: d['Asha'] = 95 → key exists, so its value is replaced

learn.reallife: DigiLocker-style apps store a citizen's documents in key-value form like {'PAN': ..., 'DL': ..., 'Aadhaar': ...}, so each document is fetched by name, not position.

A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.explain: Tuples are immutable and lists are mutable, which is exactly why only tuples are allowed as keys.
quiz.mistake: Doesn't link key rules to immutability

teach.ask: Gappu wants to store his friends' birthdays by name. Explain dictionaries: keys, values, access and updating.
teach.praise: A dictionary maps unique, immutable keys to values; I access by key, add or change with d[key] = value, and a missing key gives KeyError!
teach.nudge: Good. How do we access a value, and what happens if the key isn't there?

topics.title: Dictionary membership, traversal and core methods

learn.hook: 'Asha' in marks checks the KEYS, not the values. Forget that, and your 'search' will mysteriously fail.
points: Membership: key in d and key not in d test KEYS only. To test values use x in d.values().
Traversal: for k in d: … loops over keys (in insertion order); use d[k] for values. for k, v in d.items(): … gives key and value together.
len(d) is the number of pairs. keys(), values() and items() return views of keys, values and (key, value) tuples; wrap in list() to get a list.
get(key) returns the value or None if the key is missing (no KeyError); get(key, default) returns default instead.
update(other) adds all pairs of another dictionary, replacing values for keys that already exist.

example.q: For m = {'Asha': 92, 'Ravi': 85}, evaluate 92 in m, 'Ravi' in m, m.get('Zoya', 0), list(m.items()).
steps: in checks keys: 92 is not a key → False

learn.reallife: A railway PNR lookup is like pnr_db.get(pnr, 'Invalid PNR'): if the key exists you get the booking, otherwise a friendly message instead of a crash.

quiz.mistake: Thinks update keeps the old value or duplicates keys

quiz.mistake: Prints the tuples without unpacking

quiz.explain: Looping over a dictionary gives its keys.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the loop gives values

quiz.explain: sum() of the values 92 and 85 is 177.
quiz.mistake: Sums the keys or counts the pairs

quiz.explain: len counts the key-value pairs: 3.
quiz.mistake: Counts keys and values separately

quiz.mistake: Thinks values can't be searched

teach.ask: Gappu's check '92 in marks' keeps returning False. Explain dictionary membership, traversal and the methods keys(), values(), items(), get() and update().
teach.praise: 'in' looks at keys, values() holds the values, items() gives pairs, get() avoids KeyError and update() merges. Bug fixed!
teach.nudge: Good. Does 'in' check keys or values? Which method lets us look at values?

topics.title: More dictionary methods: del, clear, fromkeys, copy, pop, popitem, setdefault

learn.hook: pop() on a dictionary needs a key, popitem() doesn't. A dozen methods, but each has one clear job.
points: del d[key] deletes that pair (KeyError if missing); del d deletes the whole dictionary. d.clear() empties it, leaving {}.
dict.fromkeys(keys, value) creates a dictionary with the given keys all set to value (None if omitted): dict.fromkeys(['a', 'b'], 0) → {'a': 0, 'b': 0}.
d.copy() returns a new (shallow) copy. d.pop(key) removes the pair and returns its value (KeyError if missing, unless a default is given: d.pop(key, default)).
d.popitem() removes and returns the LAST inserted pair as a tuple (KeyError if d is empty). d.setdefault(key, value) returns d[key] if it exists; otherwise inserts key with value and returns value.
max(d), min(d) and sorted(d) work on the KEYS: sorted({'b': 1, 'a': 2}) → ['a', 'b'].

example.q: d = {'x': 1, 'y': 2, 'z': 3}. Do v = d.pop('y'), then p = d.popitem(). What are v, p and d?
steps: popitem() removes the last inserted pair ('z', 3) → p = ('z', 3)

learn.reallife: At the start of a school year, attendance = dict.fromkeys(roll_numbers, 0) sets every student's count to zero in one line.

games.title: Method ↔ what it returns
pairs: The value of key k (pair removed)
A new dictionary with the same pairs
A new dictionary with keys from L, all 0
d[k] if present, otherwise v (after inserting it)

quiz.mistake: Thinks pop returns the pair, or doesn't remove it

quiz.mistake: Thinks setdefault only reads

quiz.explain: max, min and sorted on a dictionary work on its keys.

quiz.q:
What is the output?
d = {'a': 1}
e = d.copy()
e['b'] = 2
print(d, e)
quiz.explain: copy() makes a separate dictionary; adding to e doesn't change d.
quiz.mistake: Thinks copy() makes an alias

quiz.q:
What is the output?

quiz.explain: del on a missing key raises KeyError.

teach.ask: Gappu mixes up pop(), popitem(), del and clear() on dictionaries. Explain each, plus fromkeys(), copy() and setdefault().
teach.praise: pop needs a key, popitem takes the last pair, del deletes, clear empties, and fromkeys, copy and setdefault build or fill. Sorted!
teach.nudge: Good. What's the difference between pop() and popitem(), and between del and clear()?

Marks lookup: marks.get(name, 'Not found') gives a safe answer for names that aren't in the dictionary.

teach.ask: Gappu wants to count how many times each letter appears in his name. Explain how to do it with a dictionary.
teach.praise: Loop over the name, and freq[ch] = freq.get(ch, 0) + 1 builds the tally automatically. Dictionary magic!

topics.title: Python modules and the math module

learn.hook: Why write a square-root function when Python already ships one? Modules are ready-made toolkits you just import.
points: A module is a .py file containing reusable functions, variables and classes. Python's standard library comes with many modules: math, random, statistics and more.
import math, then call math.sqrt(25). from math import sqrt, pi lets you call sqrt(25) directly. from math import * imports every public name (can clash with your own names, so use carefully).

math constants: math.pi ≈ 3.141592653589793, math.e ≈ 2.718281828459045. Functions: sqrt(x) (float), ceil(x) (smallest integer ≥ x), floor(x) (largest integer ≤ x), fabs(x) (absolute value as float), sin(x), cos(x), tan(x) (x in radians).
Also: factorial(n) (n!), gcd(a, b) (HCF), fmod(x, y) (float remainder, sign of x: fmod(−7, 3) = −1.0, while −7 % 3 = 2).
Built-in pow(2, 3) gives 8 (int for int arguments); math.pow(2, 3) always gives a float, 8.0.

example.q: Evaluate math.ceil(4.2), math.floor(−4.2), math.sqrt(49), math.factorial(4), math.gcd(12, 18).

learn.reallife: ISRO trajectory calculations use the same math functions (sin, cos, sqrt) that you can import in one line.

learn.hook: A Ludo app 'rolls' a die with random.randint(1, 6). Every board game app you've played leans on the random module.
points: random.random() returns a float x with 0.0 ≤ x < 1.0 (never 1.0).
random.randint(a, b) returns an integer N with a ≤ N ≤ b; BOTH ends are included.
random.randrange(start, stop, step) returns a random element of range(start, stop, step); stop is NOT included. randrange(10) gives 0 to 9.

statistics.mean(data) is the average; statistics.median(data) is the middle value of the sorted data (average of the two middle values for an even count); statistics.mode(data) is the most frequent value.
Exam tasks: predict outputs of tuple/dictionary code, find the possible outputs of random code, and write programs using dictionaries and modules.

example.q: For data = [2, 7, 4, 7, 5], find mean, median and mode.

learn.reallife: Lottery-style draws, OTP generation demos and 'shuffle' in music apps all rely on random numbers, while statistics.mean() and median() summarise exam results.

learn.hook: That embarrassing comment from Class 8 could show up when a college or employer searches your name. The internet has a long memory.
points: Digital technology makes banking, learning and communication faster and easier, but the same tools can be misused, so we must use them responsibly.
A digital footprint is the trail of data you leave behind while using the internet: posts, searches, sites visited, purchases, location and more.
Active digital footprint: data you share intentionally, such as posts, comments, emails, uploaded photos and online forms you fill.
Passive digital footprint: data collected without you actively sharing it, such as browsing history, cookies, IP address, app usage and location tracking.

Footprints are stored on your device (browser history, cookies) and on remote servers of websites and apps. Even after you delete a post, copies may remain, so footprints are very hard to erase completely.

example.q: Classify: (a) a reel you posted, (b) a shopping site remembering what you viewed, (c) a review you wrote, (d) your phone's location history.
steps: (b) Recorded through cookies while browsing → passive

learn.reallife: Recruiters and college admission teams sometimes look at applicants' public social media. A thoughtful online presence can open doors; a careless one can close them.

items: Deleting a post always removes every copy of it from the internet.

Only social media creates a digital footprint.
Searches, shopping, apps and emails also leave traces.
Your digital footprint can affect your future reputation.
Others may see and judge what you leave online.
Using the internet responsibly includes thinking about what traces you leave.
That is the core lesson of digital footprints.

topics.title: Data protection, intellectual property and licences

learn.hook: The song you're humming, the logo on your shoes and the medicine your grandmother takes are all protected by intellectual property laws.
points: Data protection keeps sensitive personal data (bank details, health records, passwords, Aadhaar) safe through encryption, authentication (passwords, OTPs, biometrics) and data-protection laws.

Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) protect creations of the mind. Copyright protects creative and literary work (books, music, software code, films). A patent protects an invention, usually for about 20 years. A trademark protects a brand's name, logo or symbol.

Violations: plagiarism (presenting someone else's work as your own without credit), copyright infringement (using protected work without permission), trademark infringement (using another's mark without permission).

Public-access licences let creators share work: Creative Commons (CC) for creative content; GNU GPL and Apache for software. FOSS (Free and Open Source Software) lets users use, study, modify and share code.
Software piracy is the unauthorised copying, distribution or use of software, and is illegal.

example.q: Classify: (a) copying a blog post into your project without credit, (b) a startup using a logo almost identical to a famous brand's, (c) selling copied DVDs of a new film.
steps: (a) Using another's words as your own → plagiarism
(b) Misusing a brand's mark → trademark infringement

topics.title: Cyber crime: hacking, phishing, ransomware and bullying

learn.hook: 'Your KYC has expired. Click here to update or your account will be blocked.' Thousands of Indians lose money to messages like this every year.
points: Cyber crime is any criminal activity in which a computer or network is used as a tool, a target, or both.

Hacking is gaining unauthorised access to a computer system. Ethical (white hat) hackers are authorised to find security weaknesses so they can be fixed; non-ethical (black hat) hackers break in to steal, damage or demand money.

Phishing: fake emails, SMSes or websites that look genuine trick people into revealing passwords, OTPs or card details. Email spoofing fakes the sender's address. Identity theft uses stolen personal details for fraud: financial (bank fraud), criminal (committing crimes in another's name) or medical (claiming treatment).
Ransomware encrypts the victim's files and demands payment (ransom) to unlock them. It spreads through malicious email attachments, fake downloads and infected websites or networks.
Eavesdropping: secretly intercepting communication on a network. Cyber trolls post provocative comments to upset people. Cyberbullying is using digital media to harass, threaten or humiliate someone.

example.q: A student gets an email from 'support@paypa1-secure.com' asking for an OTP to 'stop a payment'. Identify the crime and the red flags.
steps: The sender's address is a fake look-alike ('paypa1' uses the digit 1 in place of 'l'), made to pass as a trusted sender (spoofing)
It asks for an OTP, which no genuine company ever asks for
This is phishing aimed at financial identity theft

topics.title: Cyber safety, malware and preventing cyber crime

learn.hook: A free 'game hack' app asks for access to your SMS and contacts. That's not a game; that could be a trojan.
points: Cyber safety means using the internet safely: browsing only trusted (HTTPS) sites, protecting your identity (not over-sharing personal details), and keeping information confidential (never sharing passwords or OTPs).

Malware (malicious software) types: a virus attaches itself to files or programs and spreads when they are run; a worm copies itself across networks on its own; a trojan pretends to be useful software but harms the system; spyware secretly collects your information; adware shows unwanted advertisements.

Prevention: take regular backups; use and update antivirus software; keep the OS and apps updated; use strong, different passwords and two-factor authentication; check for HTTPS and the padlock icon; don't open unknown attachments or links.
Digital signatures verify that a document or email really comes from the claimed sender and hasn't been altered.
Report cyber crime to the local cyber cell, the national portal cybercrime.gov.in, or the helpline 1930 for financial frauds.

learn.hook: India has a law for the online world and rules for the old phones in your drawer. Both protect citizens, one from crime and one from toxins.
points: The Information Technology Act, 2000 (IT Act), amended in 2008, gives legal recognition to electronic records and digital signatures, making e-commerce and e-governance legally valid.

It lays down provisions and penalties for cyber crimes such as hacking, identity theft and publishing obscene material online. Cyber cells in police departments investigate such crimes, and the Act provided for a Cyber Appellate Tribunal to hear appeals.
E-waste is discarded electrical and electronic equipment: old phones, computers, batteries, TVs, chargers. It contains harmful substances such as lead, mercury and cadmium.
Dumping or burning e-waste releases toxins into soil, water and air, harming the health of people (especially informal workers) and the environment.

Proper management: Reduce (buy only what you need, use devices longer), Reuse (repair, donate or resell working devices), Recycle (give e-waste to authorised collection centres or recyclers, not the regular garbage).

example.q: Your family has an old laptop, a dead phone battery and a working but outdated tablet. What should you do with each?
steps: Working tablet → reuse: donate it to a school or someone who needs it
Old laptop → wipe data, then sell back or give to an authorised e-waste recycler
Dead battery → drop at an authorised collection point; never throw it in household garbage or burn it
example.answer: Reuse what works; send the rest to authorised e-waste collection

topics.title: Health, ergonomics and technology for everyone

learn.hook: Hours of online classes and scrolling can leave you with dry eyes, a stiff neck and poor sleep. Technology should fit you, not the other way round.
points: Overuse of devices can cause eye strain (dry, tired eyes), poor posture and back or neck pain, repetitive stress injuries in wrists and fingers, sleep problems, and internet addiction.

Ergonomics is designing and arranging workspaces and devices to fit the user: screen at or slightly below eye level and about an arm's length away, back supported, feet flat on the floor, wrists straight.

Healthy habits: take regular breaks (e.g. the 20-20-20 rule: every 20 minutes look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds), keep screens away before bedtime, and clean devices and keyboards regularly.

Gender issues: girls are sometimes discouraged from computing; schools should give equal access and encouragement. Disability issues: students with disabilities need assistive technology such as screen readers, Braille keyboards, speech-to-text software and screen magnifiers.
Exam-style tasks: classify scenarios (plagiarism, hacking, phishing), compare copyright and patent, analyse etiquette, and recall IT Act provisions.
